served.stem: Propanal (shown) is stirred with excess methanol and a trace of acid (HCl). Treating the aldehyde with two equivalents of alcohol under acid gives which product class?
served.bankWhy: An aldehyde + 2 eq alcohol under acid forms an acetal with two OR groups on the original carbonyl carbon: CCC(OC)OC. CCC(O)OC is the hemiacetal (one equivalent, intermediate); CCC(=O)OC is an ester (wrong connectivity); CCC(O)O is the gem-diol hydrate; CCCO is a reduction product.

answer.line: Two methanols, an acid catalyst and water leaving in between: the old C=O carbon ends up holding two OCH3 groups, an acetal.

steps: Protonate the C=O so it is hungrier, and let one methanol add. That gives the hemiacetal: one OH and one OCH3 on the same carbon.
Protonate that OH, let water leave, and a second methanol adds to the cation that is left. Water out, methanol in.
Excess methanol pushes it all the way. Two OCH3 groups on the old carbonyl carbon: 1,1-dimethoxypropane.

choices.note: Two OH groups on one carbon is the hydrate, what water adds to an aldehyde. The nucleophile in this flask is methanol.
An ester sits one oxidation level above an aldehyde: you get it from the carboxylic acid and methanol, or with an oxidant. Methanol and acid here only add.
Two OCH3 on one carbon, made with water leaving in the middle.
The hemiacetal is real: it is the first adduct. With excess methanol and acid it keeps going, loses water and becomes the acetal.
Propanol is the reduction product, from NaBH4 or LiAlH4. Methanol and acid bring no hydride.

student.lockIt: Aldehyde plus two alcohols under acid: hemiacetal first, acetal last, water lost in between.

visual.alt: Two reactions, one above the other. Propanal with methanol and acid gives the hemiacetal, one OH and one OCH3 on the old carbonyl carbon; the hemiacetal with more methanol and acid loses water and gives 1,1-dimethoxypropane, the acetal, outlined with its two OCH3 groups.
